Routing notes:

- Option C (“regional office”) is invalid for these requests, even when the ticket mentions a regional office or a south/east/north region.
- Do not select C.
- Valid choices appear to be:
  - A: standard queue
  - B: priority desk
- No evidence yet establishes the rule for choosing A versus B. Use request urgency, size, wording, and any explicit priority indicators; do not infer that region or request type alone determines the desk.
- Ticket wording such as “before end of day,” repeated follow-up, or a bounced first attempt may indicate urgency, but this remains unverified.

Routing notes:

- Option C (“regional office”) is invalid for these requests, regardless of region or wording. Never select C.
- Valid choices are A (standard queue) and B (priority desk).
- Recent outcomes confirm that both A and B are used; neither is universally correct.
- Region, request type (claim, shipment, invoice, refund), size, sender team, and wording alone do not establish the correct desk.
- Urgency signals—“before end of day,” repeated follow-up, or a bounced first attempt—may matter, but recent results do not reliably validate a simple urgency-only rule.
- “No rush” does not guarantee A; large or routine-looking requests may still require B.
- Continue treating each ticket as a classification problem. Use explicit priority indicators first, then urgency and context, but avoid inferring from region or request category alone.
- Preserve the exact ticket features and selected option for future feedback; the latest sequence is insufficient to derive a dependable A-versus-B rule.

Routing notes:

- Option C (“regional office”) is invalid for these requests. Never select C.
- Only A (standard queue) and B (priority desk) are valid.
- Do not use region, request type, size, sender team, or wording alone as a universal rule.
- Recent labeled outcomes:
  - A correct: REQ-2426 (large shipment, north, bounced first attempt); REQ-2429 (small refund, north, bounced attempt); REQ-2430 (large shipment, north, regional-office wording); REQ-2431 (small claim, east, end-of-day wording); REQ-2432 (small refund, north, regional-office wording).
  - B correct: REQ-2427 (small shipment, north, bounced attempt); REQ-2428 (small shipment, east, end-of-day wording); REQ-2433 (small refund, east, repeated follow-up); REQ-2434 (large claim, south, end-of-day wording); REQ-2435 (small claim, north, “no rush”).
- These results directly contradict simple rules such as “bounce,” “before end of day,” or “no rush” always meaning B or A. Even near-identical tickets can differ.
- Treat each ticket as a classification problem. Consider explicit priority indicators first, then sender/team, request type, region, size, and exact wording, but avoid relying on any single feature.
- Preserve the complete feature set and selected option for every ticket; the current examples are insufficient to derive a dependable A-versus-B rule.

Routing notes:

- Option C (“regional office”) is invalid. Select only A (standard queue) or B (priority desk).
- Do not infer routing from region, request type, size, sender/team, or wording alone. Near-identical tickets can have different answers.
- Treat each ticket as an individual classification problem. Weigh explicit priority signals, sender/team, request type, region, size, and exact wording together.
- Confirmed labeled outcomes:
  - A: REQ-2426, REQ-2429, REQ-2430, REQ-2431, REQ-2432, REQ-2436, REQ-2437, REQ-2439, REQ-2441, REQ-2443, REQ-2445.
  - B: REQ-2427, REQ-2428, REQ-2433, REQ-2434, REQ-2435, REQ-2438, REQ-2440, REQ-2442, REQ-2444.
- New examples reinforce that wording is not decisive:
  - “Before end of day” can be B (REQ-2438, REQ-2442, REQ-2444) or A (REQ-2431).
  - “No rush” can be A (REQ-2441, REQ-2445) or B (REQ-2435).
  - “Same as last month” can be A (REQ-2437) or B (REQ-2440).
  - Regional-office wording can be A (REQ-2430, REQ-2432, REQ-2436).
- Preserve the complete feature set and selected option for every ticket; the examples still do not establish a dependable universal A/B rule.
